པའི་ཁྱད་པར་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། ཡི་གེ་ལ་བརྟེན་པ་དང་། དོན་ལ་བརྟེན་པའོ། །ཡི་གེ་ལ་བརྟེན་པ་ནི་ཚིག་རེ་རེ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཡི་གེའི་བྱེ་བྲག་གཞན་དང་གཞན་དག་གིས་བསྐལ་པ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པར་སྟོན་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་སྤོབས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏུགས་པ་མེད་པ་ལས་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །དོན་
ལ་བརྟེན་པ་ནི་བསྐལ་པ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པར་སེམས་ཅན་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་རྣམས་སོ་སོ་ནས་ཞུ་བ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཞུས་པའི་ཞུ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ལན་ཅིག་གསུང་གཅིག་བརྗོད་པ་ཁོ་ནས་ལན་ཐེབས་པ་ལས་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ལྟར་ན་ཡི་གེ་དང་དོན་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་སྤོབས་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་གྱིས་བསམ་གྱིས་
མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ངོ་མཚར་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཆོས་སྟོན་པར་མཛད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་སྤོབས་པ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ངག་གི་སྐྱོན་{བརྫུན་,རྫུན་}དུ་སྨྲ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། སྨྲ་བར་བཅོལ་བའི་#སྐྱོན་སྤུ་ཟིང་ཞེས་བྱེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། ང་རོའི་སྐྱོན་གདངས་མི་སྙན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་
པ་དེ་དག་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་གསུང་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གསུང་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ཡིད་དུ་འོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་དབྱངས་སྙན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གསུང་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་ནི་གསུང་དབྱངས་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་ལྔ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་དྲུག་ཅུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ལས་རིག་པར་
བྱའོ། །སྐུ་བྱད་བལྟ་བས་ཆོག་མི་ཤེས་པ་དང་། སྐུ་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་འདི་གཉིས་ནི་སྐུའི་ཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་རྟེན་གྱི་#ཁྱད་པར་དང་། རང་གི་ངོ་བོའི་ཁྱད་པར་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་ནི་སྐུ་བྱད་བལྟ་བས་ཆོག་མི་ཤེས་པ་ལས་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེའི་ཡན་
ལག་དང་ཉིང་ལག་དག་ལ་ཡུན་རིང་མོ་ཞིག་ནས་མཐོང་ཡང་སྔོན་མ་མཐོང་བ་བཞིན་དུ་བལྟ་བའི་དགའ་བས་ངོམས་མི་ཤེས་པའི་སྐུ་བྱད་བལྟ་བས་ཆོག་མི་ཤེས་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །རང་གི་ངོ་བོའི་ཁྱད་པར་ནི་སྐུ་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་པ་ལས་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་ཁམས་དང་། འགྲོ་
བ་དང་། སྐྱེ་གནས་དག་ཏུ་གདུལ་བྱ་དེ་དང་དེ་དག་ལ་ཁ་དོག་དང་སྤྱོད་པ་མཐུན་པར་བསྟན་པ་དང་། ཆོས་བསྟན་པས་འདུལ་བར་མཛད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྐུ་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །འདོད་པ་དག་གིས་མ་གོས་པ། གཟུགས་དག་གིས་ཉེ་བར་མ་གོས་པ། གཟུགས་མེད་པ་དག་དང་མ་

the specific quality of eloquence is also of two kinds: that based on the letter and that based on the meaning. Regarding eloquence based on the letter, it should be known from the fact that even if he teaches for infinite eons through various distinct letters based on a single word, the Tathagata's eloquence is never exhausted. Regarding eloquence based on the meaning, it should be known from the fact that even when infinite beings individually ask infinite questions over infinite eons, all those questions are answered by the mere utterance of a single word in a single moment. Thus, because he teaches the inconceivable and wondrous Dharma through the specific qualities of eloquence based on letters and meaning, the Blessed One is called "Inconceivable Eloquence."

Because he lacks vocal faults such as speaking lies, and faults of delivery such as speaking in a way that makes hair stand on end, and vocal faults such as having an unpleasant tone, the Blessed One is called "Pure Speech." Because he is pleasing through the quality of his voice, the Blessed One is called "Melodious Voice." The qualities of his speech should be understood from his possessing the five branches or sixty branches of melodic voice.

"A physical presence that one can never look at enough" and "a peerless body" — these two show the specific basis of the body's activity and the specific quality of its essence. In that regard, the specific quality of the basis should be known from "a physical presence that one can never look at enough." Even if one looks at the major and minor limbs of the Blessed One for a very long time, one can never be satiated by the joy of looking, as if seeing them for the first time; thus, it is called "a physical presence that one can never look at enough." The specific quality of its essence should be known from "peerless body." The Blessed One is called "Peerless Body" because he shows colors and behaviors that are harmonious with those to be tamed in various realms, destinies, and birthplaces, and he tames them by teaching the Dharma.

"Unstained by desires; not tainted by forms; unmixed with the formless"
head: In that regard,
tail: — these three phrases show where the Blessed One dwells and how he performs the welfare of beings without attachment.
old_translation:
The distinction is of two kinds: that which depends on the letters and that which depends on the meaning. Regarding the dependence on letters: one should understand it from the fact that although he teaches for immeasurable eons by means of various distinct letters based on each individual word, the Tathagata's eloquence is never exhausted. 

Regarding the dependence on meaning: one should understand it from the fact that he answers all the immeasurable questions asked individually by immeasurable sentient beings over immeasurable eons with a single utterance of just one word. Thus, because he teaches the inconceivable, wonderful, and marvelous Dharma through the special quality of eloquence based on letters and meaning, the Blessed One is said to have <term>inconceivable eloquence</term>. 

Because he is free from faults of speech such as lying and the like, and faults of delivery <note>literally "making the hair stand on end"</note> such as stammering, and faults of tone such as an unpleasant voice and so forth, the Blessed One is said to have <term>pure speech</term>. 

Because he is pleasing to the mind by way of the qualities of his speech, the Blessed One is said to have a <term>melodious voice</term>. One should understand the qualities of his speech from his possession of the five and the sixty branches of melodic voice. 

The two phrases "Body that one can never tire of beholding" and "Incomparable body" show the distinction of the basis for the activities of the body and the distinction of its actual essence. Regarding the distinction of the basis, it is understood from "Body that one can never tire of beholding." This means that even if one looks at the major and minor limbs of the Blessed One for a long time, one never feels sated, but continues to look with the joy of seeing them as if for the first time. 

Regarding the distinction of the essence, it is understood from "Incomparable body." Because the Blessed One displays a color and conduct that harmonizes with those to be tamed in various realms, destinies, and birthplaces, and tames them by teaching the Dharma, he is said to have an <term>incomparable body</term>. 

"Unstained by desires," "Unshackled by forms," "Unmixed with the formless"—these three phrases show where the Blessed One dwells and how he benefits sentient beings without being attached. 

Where does he dwell to benefit beings? He dwells in the desire realm and the form realm, because there he has a connection with body and speech. He does not dwell in the formless realm; for that very reason, it is said he is "unmixed with the formless." When the Blessed One benefits beings in the desire realm, he is said to be "unstained by desires" because he is not captivated by the desires and attachments belonging to the desire realm, nor by the wrong practices of the sentient beings belonging to it. 

Even when he is in meditative absorption in the form realm, because he does not lose his focus <note>original: "mind not cast away"</note> despite demonstrating the bliss of absorption and the qualities of birth there to connect with the beings of that realm, he is said to be "unshackled by forms." "Shackled" means being closely bound; that is, being captivated by tasting the flavor of absorption and seeing the qualities of birth. Because he lacks these, he is "unshackled."
